query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-temperature exposure induces dynamic amorphization at the HEA surface, which creates an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer that enhances selective oxidation of high–oxygen-affinity elements (such as Cr or others present) to rapidly form and retain a dense, adherent protective oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with conventional grain size prior to treatment.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to high-temperature oxidative environments (e.g., air at ~900°C) for controlled durations.
generation.conditions: Comparative oxidation experiments on HEA samples that are pre-treated to promote dynamic amorphization versus samples that are processed in a way that minimizes amorphization (or alternatively, compared to inert conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer produced by dynamic amorphization, which increases grain boundary density and thereby provides abundant nucleation sites for oxide formation.
generation.mechanism: The high-temperature exposure causes local structural evolution (dynamic amorphization) at the HEA surface. This induces a high density of grain boundaries that act as fast diffusion pathways, accelerating the selective oxidation of reactive alloying elements. The resulting dense, adherent oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exhibiting dynamic amorphization will develop a more uniform, continuous, and adherent oxide scale with lower oxidation weight gains over time compared to samples that do not show this near-surface nanocrystallinity.
generation.baseline: HEA samples maintained in inert environments or processed to inhibit dynamic amorphization, wherein oxidation is limited or the oxide scale is less uniform and less adherent.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., temperatures above 800°C) for alloys with compositions amenable to forming protective oxides; it may not apply at lower temperatures or to alloys lacking sufficient high–oxygen-affinity elements.
generation.uncertainty: While the hypothesis leverages known behaviors of dynamic surface evolution and selective oxidation, the exact quantitative impact of dynamic amorphization on the kinetics and integrity of oxide scale formation remains to be rigorously determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set that is pre-treated to enhance dynamic amorphization (e.g., by controlled thermal cycling) and a control set treated to inhibit surface amorphization (e.g., via alternative processing to produce a stable microstructure). Expose both sets to oxidation at ~900°C in air for fixed durations.
measurements: Surface oxide scale morphology and continuity (via SEM/TEM)
Surface grain size and nanocrystallinity (via STEM)
Adhesion strength of the oxide layer (via scratch testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples pre-treated for dynamic amorphization do not show a significantly more uniform, continuous, and adherent oxide scale (or lower oxidation weight gain) compared to the control samples, then the mechanism linking dynamic amorphization to protective oxide formation is not supported.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
